Distance to Tech Hubs and Access to Computer Science Course in Oregon

Introduction

Broadening access to computer science education is essential to help students being ready for a tech-driven digital world. Despite years of efforts to increase Computer Science(CS) learning at the federal and state levels, the opportunity of accessing and participating CS remain unequally distributed across geographic contexts and demographic groups. Oregon is one of a few states with low CS course offerings and low participation rates compared to the national average level. According to the 2025 State of AI + CS Education report, only 56% of public high schools in Oregon offered foundation computer science during the 2023-2024 academic year, four percentage points below the national average. Previous research has identified gaps and barriers that hinder the participation of CS. However, to my knowledge, little research has explored how a school’s distance from technology centers associated with high schools’ likelihood of offering CS course, given that technology centers are considered a rich regional resource.

In this analysis, I seek to explore: Is the likelihood of offering computer science courses associated with geographic distance to technology hubs among Oregon high schools.

Specifically, I address the main question by exploring:

  1. How is Oregon high schools’ distance to the nearest technology hub distributed?

  2. Is distance to nearest tech hub associated with whether Oregon high schools offer CS courses?

  3. After accounting for enrollment, locale, and socioeconomic status, does the association change?

Method

I first combine 2021-22 Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC) and the 2022 Common Core of Data (CCD). I then use coordinates of each school and the coordinates of the three Oregon technology hubs (Portland, Salem, and Corvallis) from Google maps to construct the distance from each school to the nearest of the three technology hubs. For more details of how I construct the variables, please refer to the README.md document via my Github.

Given the main interest of this analysis, I applied a systematic filter to include only the schools that served grades 9 through 12 and were categorized as non-virtual, non-alternative, and non-juvenile-justice institutions. The completed dataset consists of 325 Oregon high schools. For the subsequent analysis, I restricted the sample to schools that have information on geographic locale, location coordinates, students eligible for Free/Reduced Price Lunch (FRPL), and student enrollment. Through this process, the main analytic sample is narrowed down to 264 high schools in Oregon.

Table 1 presents summary statistics of CS course availability by school enrollment size and geographic locale. Of 264 schools, 117 schools (44.3%) reported offering at least 1 CS course in the 2021-22 school year. Following the sample enrollment distribution, schools were categorized as very small (<=150), small (151-300), medium (300-850), and large (>850). Most schools in the sample are in rural areas (38.3%), with others in town (25.4%), suburban areas (14.4%), and cities (22.0%). About 67.2% of high schools located in city area offered CS courses, whereas it was 29.7% for high schools in rural area.

# Descriptive table
cs$locale_simplified <- relevel(factor(cs$locale_simplified), ref = "City")
cs$enrollment_cat <- relevel(factor(cs$enrollment_cat), ref = "Large (>850)")

all <- cs %>% 
  summarise(
    Variable = "All", Category = "All schools",
    'N of schools' = n(),
    'N offering CS' = sum(has_cs_course),
    '% offering CS' = round(100*mean(has_cs_course), 1),
    'Mean CS courses' = round(mean(cs_courses, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  )

by_locale <- cs %>% 
  group_by(Category = locale_simplified) %>% 
  summarise(
    'N of schools' = n(),
    'N offering CS' = sum(has_cs_course),
    '% offering CS' = round(100*mean(has_cs_course), 1),
    'Mean CS courses' = round(mean(cs_courses, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  ) %>% 
  mutate(Variable = "Location of Schools", Category = as.character(Category))

by_size <- cs %>% 
  group_by(Category = enrollment_cat) %>% 
  summarise(
    'N of schools' = n(),
    'N offering CS' = sum(has_cs_course),
    '% offering CS' = round(100*mean(has_cs_course), 1),
    'Mean CS courses' = round(mean(cs_courses, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  ) %>% 
  mutate(Variable = "Enrollment size", Category = as.character(Category))

bind_rows(all, by_locale, by_size) %>% 
  gt(groupname_col = "Variable", rowname_col = "Category") %>% 
  tab_header(
    title = "Table 1.
    Descriptive Statistics on Oregon High Schools and CS Course Availability (2021-22)"
  ) %>% 
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Note: Summary statistics for 264 Oregon public high schools with complete data on all study variables. CS course and Enrollment were retrieved from 2021-22 Civil Rights Data Collection (CRDC). Enrollment is categorized as Very Small (<=150 students), Small (151-300 students), Medium (300 – 850 students), and Large (> 850 students) based on the sample distribution. Values are rounded to 1 digit. The Geographic locale information was retrieved from the 2022 Common Core Data (CCD). ")

Outcome Variable

The key dependent variable in this analysis is a dichotomous outcome, whether schools offer CS courses. Schools reported having at least 1 CS course are marked as 1, else 0. Table 1 reports the CS offering status by enrollment size and locale, showing that most large schools or schools in city areas offer CS courses.

Predictor Variables

The primary predictor of interest in this analysis is schools’ distance to the nearest technology hubs. To construct this variable, I first obtained the geographic coordinates of Portland, Salem, and Corvallis because these three cities are the home of three tech centers recognized at both the state and federal levels.

The coordinates of each city were retrieved from Google Maps, using the city center coordinates as the representative point for each tech hub. I calculated distance using the haversine formula, which accounts for Earth’s spherical shape when computing great-circle distances between geographical points (Robusto, 1957). This process produced distance variables representing each school’s proximity to every technology hub, from which I obtain the primary predictor variable: the distance from each school to the nearest of the three technology hubs.

How is Oregon high schools’ distance to the nearest technology hub distributed?

To explore my first area of interest in this topic, I graph a bar chart to illustrate the distribution of

cs %>% 
  add_count(locale_simplified) %>% 
  mutate(locale_n = paste0(locale_simplified, "(n =", n, ")")) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = distance_to_nearest_hub)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#1E6291", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ locale_simplified) +
  labs(title = "Figure 1. Distance to the nearest technology hub by school locale (2021-22)",
    x = "Distance to nearest tech hub (miles)",
    y = "Number of schools"
  )+
  theme_bw()
